title: An hour after the pacing wires came out
objective: Recognize cardiac tamponade from hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension and pulsus paradoxus, and escalate for drainage

sources.cite: Progressive care nursing certification exam handbook and test plan: Cardiovascular (20% of the exam)
sources.note: Relayed from the PCCN course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/pccn.ts), which read the handbook 2026-11-14, not re-read: Cardiovascular is the largest clinical category. Scope only.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.cite: Schulz-Menger J, Collini V, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041
sources.note: Relayed from the CCRN Adult case tamponade-after-cabg (read 2026-11-09), not re-read: tamponade is an effusion impairing diastolic filling until cardiac output falls, possible at 200-300 mL of blood; after cardiac surgery an effusion may be loculated; a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo; drainage, surgical drainage preferred for bleeding into the pericardium; avoid diuretics and positive-pressure ventilation; temporary fluid support. A European guideline: the unit's policy follows it.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

brief.situation: 10:20 on a cardiac progressive care unit. You are the nurse for Mr. Haines, 70, on day 4 after coronary bypass surgery. His temporary epicardial pacing wires were pulled at 09:15. The aide says he 'won't settle and looks gray'.
handover: Before the wires: blood pressure 124/72, heart rate 84 in sinus rhythm. Aspirin; prophylactic heparin under the skin.
The hospitalist covering the unit has written 'IV furosemide for signs of fluid overload' on his orders after he gained a kilogram overnight.

Unit policy for a suspected complication after wire removal: rapid response and the cardiac surgeon at once; an echo at the bedside; a crystalloid bolus may be given to support the pressure while they come.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what is happening and who must come.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Blood collects in the pericardium after wire removal: about 1/40 of the way to arrest per minute. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Systolic support from a crystalloid bolus while drainage is arranged. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A diuretic in tamponade: the preload the heart depends on falls. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of pulseless electrical activity. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Rapid response and the surgeon within 5 minutes of the first sign (unit policy).
Surgeon, bedside echo and the move to the operating room for drainage: about 10 min.

then.log: Neck veins distended to the jaw sitting up. Heart sounds distant and muffled. Lungs clear to the bases.
Pulsus paradoxus {pulsus|0dp} mm Hg: the systolic falls that much with each breath in. Pulse pressure {pp|0dp}.
Sinus tachycardia {hr}, low-voltage QRS throughout. No new ST elevation.
"I just feel awful, like I can't get comfortable." The removal note says both wires came out intact at 09:15; no bleeding noted.

why.question: Mr. Haines is restless and gray an hour after his pacing wires came out. What is happening, and who needs to come?

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Cardiac tamponade from bleeding after wire removal: falling pressure and rising heart rate with distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus over 10, clear lungs; not fluid overload.
parts.modelAnswer: Hypotension and tachycardia with distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and a pulsus paradoxus over 10, an hour after his wires came out, is cardiac tamponade. His lungs are clear, so this isn't fluid overload.

parts.label: Who and what
parts.criteria: Rapid response and the cardiac surgeon now for echo and drainage; a fluid bolus to support the pressure; no diuretic (it removes the filling the heart depends on).
parts.modelAnswer: Rapid response and the surgeon now for an echo and drainage. A fluid bolus to hold his pressure. The furosemide stays in the drawer: a diuretic takes away the filling his squeezed heart needs.

noProgress.rationale: Suspected tamponade still undrained an hour on is harm here.

diuretic.label: Collapse after the diuretic
diuretic.when: not isNull(lasixAt) and t >= timeAt(lasixAt) + 120 and inClinic
diuretic.narrative: Blood pressure {sbp}/{dbp}: the diuretic took the filling his compressed heart depended on. Rapid response is called to a crashing patient.

pea.label: Pulseless electrical activity
pea.narrative: The monitor still shows a rhythm, but there is no pulse. The tamponade has stopped his heart filling. A code is called.

drained.label: Tamponade recognized and drained

expertPath.text: Gray and restless after wire removal: neck veins, heart sounds, lungs. Distended, muffled, clear.
Pulsus paradoxus over 10. Rapid response and the cardiac surgeon now.
A bolus to hold the pressure. The furosemide is held.
SBAR to the surgeon; the echo confirms; he goes for drainage.

diuretic.headline: A diuretic in tamponade
diuretic.body: Distended neck veins with clear lungs and hypotension after wire removal is tamponade until an echo says otherwise. Diuretics take away the filling the compressed heart needs.

pea.headline: PEA
pea.body: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds after wire removal need the surgeon and drainage within minutes.

drained.headline: Recognized and drained
drained.body: You read the triad and the pulsus, held the diuretic, supported the pressure and called rapid response and the surgeon at once. That is the expert path.

drainedLate.headline: Drained, with delays
drainedLate.body: Check how long the call took and whether pulsus paradoxus was measured.

time_up.headline: Still undrained
time_up.body: Suspected tamponade needs drainage within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: An hour after epicardial pacing wires come out, falling pressure and a rising heart rate with distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and a pulsus paradoxus over 10 mm Hg, with clear lungs, is cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. Rapid response and the cardiac surgeon come now for a bedside echo and drainage; a fluid bolus supports the pressure meanwhile; the ordered furosemide is held, because a diuretic removes the filling the compressed heart depends on.

becksQ.ask: While you assess: which findings together suggest tamponade?

choices.label: Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, with pulsus paradoxus
Crackles to the mid-lungs and pink frothy sputum
High blood pressure and a slow pulse

becksQ.explain: An effusion that impairs filling lowers cardiac output; it is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo.
